column1: # Model scope: which production functions are bound to a TLA+ spec.
# scripts/ci/check-model-scope.sh reads this and, for a change that touches one
# of these functions, asks that the spec and its fixture move too. It proves
# nothing -- it turns "the model quietly stopped tracking the code" into a
# review prompt. A change that legitimately does not affect the model passes by
# saying so: put `Model-scope-ok: <reason>` in a commit message or the PR body.
# What is NOT here matters as much as what is, so unmodelled machines are rows
# check-model-scope.sh enforces completeness mechanically: every function under
# internal/ named compute[A-Z]*, step[A-Z]*, or set*Rollup (tests excluded)
# must appear in this manifest, either bound to a spec or UNMODELLED with a
# non-empty reason. A new state machine therefore cannot ship without either a
# spec binding or a written-down decision not to have one. Rows for functions
# outside the naming convention (stsMatchesSpec, Stamp, checkDrainComplete) are
# listed for visibility even though the scan would not demand them.
# So "the TLA+ suite passes" means "the modelled machines still agree with
# their specs", not "this change is verified". Modelling a machine means
# writing a spec for it; SigningKeyRotation.tla is the smallest worked example,

column4: the agent's hold path is modelled by formal/WakeAgentHold.tla but deliberately not bound to Go: the tracker state is unexported in-memory bookkeeping in a package that must not import controller-runtime, so TLC alone checks Inv_NoStrandedWaiter / Inv_WaiterRefsAccurate and internal/wakeagent's unit tests hold the Go line; binding it needs an exported test seam on the tracker
class merge and drift detection (stsMatchesSpec and the effective* resolvers) are stateless comparators; the specs abstract them as the specVer input
drain probing and its timeouts are deliberately deferred: fuzzed time is the highest false-positive axis
